tonight.headline: You are 34.7 points from safe, and you cannot add one of them
body: Your nine starters are finished on 125.1. Nicky Jam sit on 90.4 with two Kansas City players still to play tonight: Kenneth Walker III and the Chiefs defence, projected 14.7 and 6.2. They need 34.7 from a 20.9 projection.
There is nothing to set. Every one of your players has played. Read the rest of this for Week 2 — and read the waiver card first, because that claim processes at 01:00 Wednesday.

case.label: The script that beats you
case.body: Kansas City host Denver and Patrick Mahomes is starting. The version where Nicky Jam get 34.7 is a Chiefs blowout: the defence clears 15 on a pick-six or two turnovers, and Walker takes fourth-quarter carries with the game gone. Rashee Rice is confirmed to play after full participation in every Week 1 practice, which pushes Kansas City's production toward the pass and away from Walker's receiving work.

case.label: Correcting what you read this morning
case.body: The brief published at 22:09 UTC told you this was final and that you had won 152.9 to 90.4. Both are wrong. 152.9 counted Isaiah Likely's 27.8 from your bench, and two Kansas City starters on the other roster have not kicked off. The number that matters is 125.1 and the game is live.

case.label: Falsified if
case.body: Walker breaks one long touchdown run, or Kansas City return a turnover for a score. Either single play puts 34.7 inside reach, which is why 91% is not 100%.

doFirst.title: Claim Jalen Coker — he was in a walking boot today, claim him anyway
doFirst.subtitle: Drop Stafford. Chem priority resets weekly, so being wrong about this costs you nothing that lasts.

case.label: The player
case.body: Eight catches on nine targets for 138 yards and two touchdowns in Week 1, leading Carolina in every receiving category while Tetairoa McMillan was quiet until the game was decided. He is rostered in 50.7% of leagues. In a ten-team league that is an ownership anomaly, not a verdict — somebody here simply has not looked.

case.label: What changed since this morning
case.body: Coker was photographed in a walking boot on Monday with an ankle tweak. He told reporters he does not expect to miss time, and NBC Sports, Yahoo and DraftKings Network all carry the same line from him. ESPN has now flipped him to QUESTIONABLE in your league file. This morning's version of this card did not know any of that.

case.label: Why the boot does not stop the claim
case.body: Carolina's first Week 2 practice report lands Wednesday, which is after your claim processes at 01:00. You are claiming before the evidence arrives and there is no way around that. In Chem it is still the right trade: waiver priority resets every week, so a claim that turns out badly costs you a roster spot for four days rather than a season of priority. This is the exact move that would be wrong in IPADE and is cheap here.

case.label: The collision with your trade
case.body: This claim drops Matthew Stafford at 01:00 Wednesday, and Stafford is half of the offer in the card below. Send that message first. If JuiceJam accept before Wednesday, McLaurin and Stafford both leave and this claim needs no drop at all — do not replace Stafford with Monangai, who scored 20.4 and whose thesis just proved right.

case.label: Falsified if
case.body: Coker is limited or does not practise in Carolina's Wednesday report, or he carries an injury designation into Sunday; or McMillan reasserts as the clear alpha and Coker's target share falls under roughly 18% across Weeks 2 and 3.

doFirst.deadlineLabel: Stafford leaves your roster at 01:00 Wednesday
doFirst.title: Send the JuiceJam offer today, not tomorrow
doFirst.subtitle: McLaurin and Stafford for DeVonta Smith. Your own waiver claim deletes Stafford in 27 hours.

case.label: Why today
case.body: This is a deadline you created yourself. The Coker claim processes at 01:00 Wednesday and takes Stafford with it. After that the offer below is McLaurin for DeVonta Smith straight up, which JuiceJam have no reason to take. The window is tonight and tomorrow.

case.label: What they actually need
case.body: JuiceJam start Jared Goff at 277.8 for the season, the second-weakest starting quarterback in this league. Stafford projects 303.4 here. That is the whole reason this clears for them — they are not doing you a favour on the receiver.

case.label: Why Smith is the buy
case.body: DeVonta Smith is Philadelphia's undisputed number one receiver now that A.J. Brown is in New England, and he returned three scoreless catches in Week 1. That is the shape you want: the role is confirmed by reporting and the box score is not. He is their slot-4 starter, so you are asking for a starter — it is survivable for them only because D.J. Moore sits on their bench at 209.0 and backfills the slot.

case.label: The honest risk
case.body: Recomputed from this afternoon's snapshot: plus 21.8 to you, plus 3.8 to them on season projections. On this week's projections alone it is minus 0.9 for them. This offer clears on the season horizon and does not clear on a one-week one, which is the opposite of the usual warning and you should expect a manager who only checks this week to decline it.

case.label: Falsified if
case.body: JuiceJam decline; or the Coker claim processes at 01:00 Wednesday and removes Stafford from the offer; or Stefon Diggs's target share in Washington collapses after Week 3 and McLaurin's role recovers, which would make selling him at his lowest point the mistake.

doFirst.title: Start Likely over Pitts in Week 2
doFirst.subtitle: Still the call, and closer than this morning said — the Giants drew a top-three streaming defence.

case.label: Who is throwing
case.body: This is the whole card. Atlanta have no Week 2 starter. Kevin Stefanski said Monday he has no updates on either Tua Tagovailoa's oblique or Michael Penix Jr. and no timeline for naming anyone; Ian Rapoport put Penix at next week or Week 3. Cooper Rush went 12 of 22 for 143 yards with one touchdown and two interceptions in a 20-13 loss. The Giants' quarterback is settled — Jaxson Dart — and Likely is his safety valve.

case.label: Both roles are intact
case.body: Pitts did not lose his job: he ran a route on 81% of Atlanta's dropbacks, tied seventh among Week 1 tight ends, on one target that was an underthrown deep ball. Likely is the Giants' second passing option behind Malik Nabers and arguably the first while Nabers is less than 100%. This is a choice between two working players, not a rescue.

case.label: What got worse today
case.body: The Giants draw the Rams in Week 2 and the Rams are a top-three streaming defence this week even with Myles Garrett hurt; Pitts gets Carolina at home. On matchup alone this call flips. It does not flip, because who is under centre outranks who is across the line, and Atlanta cannot tell you who is under centre.

case.label: Where I disagree with the market
case.body: ESPN's own season projection prefers Pitts 181.4 to Likely's 156.2 and ranks him TE7 against TE12. I am taking the other side on the quarterback and I am less confident than the card you read this morning was. If you want a single trigger: Atlanta's Wednesday practice report.

case.label: Falsified if
case.body: Atlanta name Tua or Penix as the starter by Friday and Pitts clears five targets in Week 2; or Pitts out-scores Likely in two of the next three weeks; or Nabers reaches full health and Likely's route share drops below roughly 60%.

whatWentWrong.title: Your tight end scored nothing and the replacement was already on your bench
whatWentWrong.lead: Pitts 0.0 on a 9.8 projection. Likely 27.8 on a 9.5 projection, benched.

case.label: It was not a lineup mistake
case.body: Check the clock before you blame yourself. Atlanta kicked off at 17:00 UTC and Pitts locked. You added Likely at 19:03 UTC, two hours after that. There was no moment on Sunday when you could have started Likely instead — the tight end slot was already frozen with Pitts in it.

case.label: What the real error was
case.body: The add was right and a day late. Likely was available all Saturday. The cost of adding a player after the early kickoffs is that he cannot enter your lineup until the following week, which is exactly what happened.

case.label: What it connects to
case.body: The Week 2 card above is this week's version of the same decision, made in time instead of after the fact.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Nothing about Sunday. If Atlanta name a real quarterback by Friday, the Week 2 version of this call changes; Sunday's does not.

whatWentWrong.title: The brief published at 22:09 today had your score wrong and deleted your trade
whatWentWrong.lead: It said you had won 152.9 to 90.4. You are winning 125.1 to 90.4 with two of their players still to play.

case.label: The arithmetic
case.body: 152.9 is 125.1 plus Isaiah Likely's 27.8. Likely was on your bench. Bench points do not count, and that run added them to your starting total.

case.label: The bigger loss
case.body: That run also published an empty trades section. The McLaurin-and-Stafford-for-DeVonta-Smith offer was written into the decision log at 13:18 this morning, nobody at JuiceJam has seen it, and it vanished from your screen. It is restored below and it is the second card above.

case.label: What it connects to
case.body: Directly to the trade card. A proposal nobody has declined is still live, and a brief that quietly drops it is worse than a brief that argues against it.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Nothing — this is arithmetic, and it is corrected. The reason it is here rather than buried is that you may have already acted on the wrong number.

whatWentWrong.title: Brian Thomas Jr.'s thesis calls him Jacksonville's WR1. The depth chart is not that simple.
whatWentWrong.lead: Jacksonville list three first-string receivers by alignment, not a one-two-three. Thomas is first-string at his spot.

case.label: What the depth chart actually says
case.body: Jacksonville's first published depth chart of the 2026 regular season names three first-string receivers by where they line up: Parker Washington in the slot, Brian Thomas Jr. at left with Travis Hunter second behind him, and Jakobi Meyers at right. It is an alignment chart, not a hierarchy. Reading it as WR1-WR2-WR3 — which is how a quick summary of that page renders it, and how I first read it today — invents a ranking the Jaguars did not publish.

case.label: So where does the thesis stand
case.body: Unresolved, not broken. The condition is that Meyers or Washington passes him on the depth chart, and neither has: they hold different jobs. But the thesis's phrasing, 'listed WR1 for Jacksonville ahead of Meyers', claims more than the chart supports and should be read as 'first-string at his alignment'.

case.label: The evidence that actually matters
case.body: Three catches for 40 in a game Jacksonville led 24-0 at half, with Lawrence attempting only 23 passes in a blowout. That is thin rather than damning. He also left with a shoulder and returned in the second quarter; it is his second shoulder scare of the year, and no imaging and no Jaguars statement have been published.

case.label: What it connects to
case.body: It is why the waiver claim above is Coker and not Meyers, and why Thomas is not the drop on any card this run — he arrived on 12 September, so the churn rule closes that slot unless he is ruled out.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: Target share under roughly 18% through Week 3, a Jaguars statement putting the shoulder in doubt, or Meyers out-targeting him in Week 2.

case.label: Why it works for you
case.body: Recomputed from this afternoon's snapshot, not carried from this morning: your optimal season lineup goes 2070.3 to 2092.1, plus 21.8. Smith takes the RB/WR flex from McLaurin at 240.1 against 218.3, and Stafford leaves a bench seat he was never going to leave on merit.

case.label: Why it works for them
case.body: JuiceJam's starting quarterback is Jared Goff at 277.8, second-weakest in the league. Stafford is 303.4. Their optimal lineup goes 1966.4 to 1970.2. Smith is their slot-4 starter and D.J. Moore backfills from their bench at 209.0, which is the only reason asking for a starter is survivable here.

case.label: The sell on McLaurin
case.body: Washington signed Stefon Diggs in August into a room that already had Deebo Samuel and Zach Ertz. Diggs went 4/55/1 in his debut; McLaurin returned 3.4 on a 12.3 projection with Philadelphia bracketing him. He is 30, coming off a quad injury that ended a four-year run of 17-game seasons. This is selling a name at the moment the role is being shared.

case.label: The buy on Smith
case.body: Not the box score — the role. A.J. Brown is in New England and Smith is the undisputed number one in Philadelphia, and he still produced three scoreless catches in Week 1. Strong usage with a bad result is the buy signal; a hot week on low volume is the sell signal. This is the first one.

case.label: The risk, stated plainly
case.body: Three. It clears on the season horizon and not on a one-week one — minus 0.9 for them this week — so a manager checking only Week 2 declines it. It asks for a starter, which reads as aggressive however it is priced. And every season number here comes from a seasonProj field that has not moved by a single decimal between a 13:18 UTC snapshot and a 22:16 UTC one, with a full week of football in between; treat the totals as indicative and the structural argument as the real case.

case.label: Falsified if
case.body: They decline; or the Coker claim processes at 01:00 Wednesday and removes Stafford from the offer; or Diggs's target share collapses after Week 3 and McLaurin's role recovers, which would make this a sale at the bottom.

trades.sources: RotoBaller · Northeast Times · NBC Sports · Commanders.com · ESPN
trades.copyText: Hey - you're starting Goff at QB and I've got Stafford sitting behind Josh Allen doing nothing for me. Would you do Terry McLaurin + Matthew Stafford for DeVonta Smith? Straight up you're getting the better end at QB (Stafford's a clear upgrade on Goff for the rest of the year) plus McLaurin, and DJ Moore slides into Smith's spot for you. I need a flex more than I need a backup QB. Let me know either way - happy to tweak it.

worthALook.name: Jakobi Meyers
worthALook.lead: Rostered in four of five leagues nationally and free here. The reason to pass is your own roster, not his.

case.label: The anomaly
case.body: 79.1% owned and sitting on waivers in a ten-team league is the strongest single signal a wire gives you. Somebody dropped a player four out of five leagues want.

case.label: The number that kills it
case.body: Jacksonville's depth chart lists him first-string at right receiver — a real job, not a demotion — but you already own the Jaguars defence, Brian Thomas Jr. and Bhayshul Tuten. Meyers would be your fourth Jacksonville player, and he is the third mouth in that receiver room behind Thomas and Parker Washington on targets, not on the chart.

case.label: The stacking problem
case.body: You are three deep on Jacksonville. In Week 7 the Jaguars are on bye and your defence, Tuten and Thomas all disappear on the same Sunday. A fourth Jaguar makes a known problem worse for a player the team lists third.

case.label: When to act
case.body: If Parker Washington misses time, or if Meyers out-targets Thomas in Week 2, he stops being a stack and starts being the Jacksonville receiver to own. Until then he is a watch.

worthALook.name: Chris Rodriguez Jr.
worthALook.lead: Jacksonville's depth chart now names him and your Bhayshul Tuten co-starters. Read this as a warning about Tuten first.

case.label: What the depth chart says
case.body: The Jaguars list 'Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr.' as co-starters at running back, with LeQuint Allen Jr. and Ameer Abdullah behind them. That is not a lead back and a handcuff; that is a stated committee.

case.label: Why it matters to your roster
case.body: Tuten carries a 205.2 season projection that assumes a workload the team has not given him. In full PPR a back who splits carries and does not own third downs collects the least valuable touches available. This is the number to be sceptical of, not Rodriguez's.

case.label: The number that kills the add
case.body: 73.1 for the season and 5.8 this week. He is the wrong half of the committee to own unless Tuten is hurt, and claiming him would be handcuffing your own uncertainty rather than fixing it.

case.label: When to act
case.body: If Tuten misses a game, or if Rodriguez takes the goal line twice in three weeks, he becomes the Jacksonville back worth a free Chem claim. Not before.

doNotChase.name: Xavier Worthy
doNotChase.lead: A 75%-rostered receiver is a free agent in your league until Kansas City kick off tonight. Leave him.

case.label: Why he is free at all
case.body: Every free agent in your league right now is a Kansas City or Denver player, because those are the only two teams whose game has not kicked off. At 00:15 UTC tonight that ends and Worthy becomes a waiver claim like everyone else. This is a clock, not an opportunity.

case.label: The number that kills it
case.body: You cannot add him. All fourteen of your players have kicked off, so there is nobody to drop. The only seat that opens before Wednesday is Stafford's, and Stafford is simultaneously the Coker drop and half the JuiceJam offer. Worthy would cost you the better of those two.

case.label: It has already been tried here
case.body: On 13 September a run recommended exactly this — add Worthy, drop Isaiah Likely. Likely then scored 27.8. Your own decision log carries it as WRONG, and the bench slot it touched had already gone Goedert to Allgeier to Likely in five days.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: If the JuiceJam trade lands, two seats open at once and a free 75%-owned receiver becomes a real question — by which point he is a Chem waiver claim, which costs nothing anyway. Revisit Wednesday, not tonight.

doNotChase.name: Mark Andrews
doNotChase.lead: The best player available on your wire, and structurally unusable on this roster.

case.label: He is genuinely good
case.body: 83.2% owned, 169.4 for the season, a real starting tight end sitting on waivers in a ten-team league. Baltimore rank fifth in the Week 2 defence rankings and face New Orleans, so the offence should be playing with a lead.

case.label: The number that kills it
case.body: Chem's flex is RB/WR only. A second tight end cannot enter your lineup, and you already carry two in Pitts and Likely. Andrews would be your third, and the third one is worth zero points per week by construction.

case.label: The precedent, in both directions
case.body: Your log says this structural argument was used on 13 September to justify dropping Likely, who then scored 27.8, and it is recorded as WRONG — because it valued the slot rather than the player. That lesson applies to dropping someone good. It does not apply to adding a third player at a position that starts one.

case.label: What would change it
case.body: A trade that moves Pitts, or an injury to both tight ends. Until then he is somebody else's problem to solve.

cannotSee.body: Every season total quoted here comes from a seasonProj field. Two snapshots, 13:18 and 22:16 UTC today, give byte-identical values for Tuten 205.2, Golden 190.3, Mayer 85.0 and Lloyd 135.6 — with a full week of football played in between and Josh Allen 16 points over his projection. That is consistent with a preseason artifact. Treat every season number in this brief, including the trade valuation, as August's opinion until it is seen to move.

cannotSee.label: Rival claims are invisible
cannotSee.body: ESPN only ever returns your own waiver claims. Someone else may be claiming Coker at 01:00 Wednesday and there is no way to know. There is deliberately no fallback card this run: the only fallback worth making would drop Brian Thomas Jr., who arrived on 12 September, and re-adding Diggs two days after cutting him is the churn your log has already punished twice.
